S1.title: Statistics Estimators And Bias
S1.text:
1. Bias of an Estimator
In statistics the bias of an estimator is its expected value minus the true parameter it estimates. An
estimator with zero bias is called unbiased. The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the
population mean. The sample variance that divides by n - 1 is an unbiased estimator of the
population variance, while dividing by n gives a biased estimator that underestimates the
population variance by the factor (n - 1) / n.
Estimator bias is a property of a calculation procedure over repeated samples. It is different from
sampling bias, which is a flaw in how the data were collected, for example surveying only
volunteers.

S3.title: Statistics Estimators And Bias
S3.text:
3. The Bootstrap
The bootstrap estimates the uncertainty of a statistic by resampling. Draw n observations with
replacement from the original sample of size n, compute the statistic, and repeat this B times, for
example B = 1000. The spread of the B statistics approximates the sampling variability.
A bootstrap percentile interval for 95% confidence uses the 2.5th and the 97.5th percentiles of the
B bootstrap statistics. The bootstrap needs no formula for the standard error, which makes it useful
for medians and other awkward statistics.

S4.title: Statistics Confusable Terms
S4.text: learning course). normal: the normal distribution is the bell curve. It does not mean "typical" or "healthy" values.  standardization: in this course standardization means converting values to z-scores with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. adjusted R squared: adjusted R2 = 1 - (1 - R2) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1) where p is the number of predictors. Plain R2 never decreases when a predictor is added to the model, so adjusted R2 is used to compare models of different sizes. sample: in statistics a sample is a subset drawn from a population. In machine learning courses a sample often means a single row of data.

S5.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
S5.text:
Problem 1: Sample versus Population Variance
Question. For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 compute the population variance and the sample variance.
Solution. The mean is 40 / 8 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32. The population variance is 32 / 8 = 4 and the population standard deviation is 2. Treated as a sample, the sample variance is 32 / 7, about 4.571, and the sample standard deviation is about 2.138. The sample version is larger because it divides by n - 1 instead of n.
